title: Searching by halving: where the bug hides
instruction: Step through a search in a sorted list. The program doesn’t look at the numbers in order, but always in the middle, and throws half away. Keep track of the variables low, high and mid. Careful: in the third round there is a bug hidden in the code.

steps.why: 21 < 30, so thirty can only be to the right. The program throws away the left half, 21 included: low = 5 + 1 = 6.

steps.q: Where does the program look, and what does it find?
steps.why: (6 + 9) / 2 = 7.5, rounded down 7. list[7] = 30. Two comparisons were enough. Searching from the start would have needed seven.
30 > 26, so the number we want would have to be to the left of position 7: high = 7 - 1 = 6.

steps.input: Next step: mid = 6, list[6] = 25 < 26, so low = 7. Now low = 7, high = 6.
options: it ends and the program returns “not found”
steps.why: The condition low ≤ high doesn’t hold: 7 ≤ 6 is false. The stretch where the number could be is empty. The program ends after a finite number of steps, even though it didn’t find the number.

steps.input: Target 40. After two steps low = 7, high = 9, mid = 8, list[8] = 34.
steps.q: What does the line with the bug do?
steps.why: 34 < 40, so low = mid runs. In this code the + 1 is missing, so low = 8, not 9.

options: mid is 8 again and the program loops forever
mid is 9 and the program finds 40
steps.why: (8 + 9) / 2 = 8.5, down to 8. Again 34 < 40, again low = 8. Nothing changes and the loop runs forever. The algorithm broke finiteness. Only a test with the number at the very end of the list finds this bug: an edge case.

steps.input: The fixed code (with + 1), the sorted list has 1000 numbers
steps.q: At most how many times does the program look into the list?
steps.why: Each comparison at least halves the stretch: 1000, 500, 250, 125, 62, 31, 15, 7, 3, 1. That is 10 looks, because 2 to the power of 10 is 1024. For a million numbers, 20 are enough. Searching from the start may need a million.

debrief: Halving the interval is one of the most powerful algorithms there is: each step throws away half of the possibilities. But it only works on a sorted list, and only if the stretch really gets smaller at every step. A single missing + 1 turns a fast algorithm into an endless loop. That’s why you test the edges too: the first number, the last number and a number that isn’t in the list.
